subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Tuesday evening. Today was the maths test and my hands were slippery and my forehead was wet. Neelam sat next to me and whispered, "Are you hot?" I said, "A bit." Actually the fan wasn't working, and also I was very scared about fractions. After the test I ran to the playground for football and sweated even more, but that felt good, not scary. Amma says sweat can mean lots of things, and you have to look at where you are and how you feel. At night I had no fever, so it was just a hot day and nerves. I'll do better next time. — Gargi

qa.q: Why was the fan not helping in the classroom?
qa.a: The fan wasn't working.

qa.q: What might have made Gargi sweat during the test, and how did Gargi tell the difference from football?
qa.a: The hot room and fear about fractions both could have made Gargi sweat. Sweating at football felt good and not scary, so the setting and Gargi's feelings helped tell them apart.

qa.q: What could Gargi do next time Gargi gets nervous before a test?
qa.a: Gargi could breathe slowly and tell someone about feeling nervous, and remember that sweat alone doesn't tell the cause.

qa.q: How might Neelam have seen Gargi's sweating?
qa.a: Neelam asked "Are you hot?", so Neelam guessed it was the heat. Neelam may not have known Gargi was also scared.

grounding: A child sweats from heat, exercise and nervousness before a test; the cause cannot be told from sweat alone, so the setting and other signs matter.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: On the sports day at the village school, Harsha's face was dripping by the time the relay ended. Gargi, the PT teacher, looked at him. It was noon in the hot dusty field and he'd just run. She didn't think much. Later in class, Harsha sweated again while sitting still, and his hands kept turning the corner of his notebook. She recalled that the maths test began in ten minutes. She asked, "Are you all right?" He said, "A bit nervous." Gargi nodded and told him to take a sip of water and a slow breath. She knew the same sweat could mean heat, running or nerves.

qa.q: What did Harsha do with his notebook while sweating in class?
qa.a: His hands kept turning the corner of his notebook.

qa.q: Why did Gargi treat Harsha's sweat at noon differently from the sweat in class, and what was Harsha feeling in class?
qa.a: At noon he had just run in the heat, so the setting explained it. In class he was still and fidgeting before the test, and he said he was nervous.

qa.q: What could Gargi do to help Harsha before the test?
qa.a: Have him take a sip of water and a slow breath, and keep checking in, as she did.

qa.q: How might Harsha feel about being asked if he is all right?
qa.a: He answered honestly that he was nervous, so he may feel relieved that his teacher noticed instead of assuming.

grounding: A school-age child sweats from heat, exercise and nervousness before a test, and the teacher reads the setting and other signs.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
The maths test in the Mexico City school started right after recess. Javier slid into his seat, shirt stuck to his back, drops of sweat running down his temples.
Wei, at the next desk, whispered, "Are you okay? You look really nervous."
Javier grinned and wiped his forehead with his sleeve. "Nervous? I just ran the whole yard six times. We won the race!"
Wei looked again. Javier's face was red, not pale, and he was breathing hard but smiling. His pencil was steady.
"Oh," Wei said. "I thought it was the test."
"The test is easy," Javier said, fanning himself with the question paper. "The race was hard."
By the second question, his breathing had slowed and the sweat had dried.

qa.q: How many times did Javier run the yard?
qa.a: Six times.

qa.q: What was Wei thinking when seeing Javier's sweat?
qa.a: Wei felt concerned and assumed Javier was nervous about the test, reading the sweat as worry.

qa.q: How could Wei have read the situation more accurately?
qa.a: By noticing the setting, right after recess, and other signs like a red face, a smile and a steady pencil, which point to exercise, not nerves.

qa.q: How might Javier see Wei's question?
qa.a: Javier seemed amused and a bit surprised, since he felt happy from the race, not worried.

grounding: A child's sweating after recess is read as test nerves, but the setting and other signs point to exercise.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
It was a cool morning in the Shillong school, and everyone wore sweaters. But Tenzin sat by the window with sweat on his forehead, and his hair was damp.
Lakshmi Ma'am noticed. Was he nervous about the Hindi dictation? He'd been worried last week. But he wasn't fidgeting, and he hadn't touched his tiffin. He rested his head on the desk.
She knelt beside him. "Tenzin, how are you feeling?"
"Hot," he mumbled. "And my head hurts."
Ma'am felt his forehead with the back of her hand. It was warm. She sent another child to fetch the school nurse and phoned his father.
The nurse took Tenzin to the sick room to lie down until his father came to take him home.

qa.q: What did the other children wear that morning?
qa.a: Sweaters.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi Ma'am thinking when she saw Tenzin sweating?
qa.a: She felt concerned and was unsure at first, wondering if he was nervous about the dictation, but the cool weather and other signs made her worry he was ill.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi Ma'am do that fits the situation?
qa.a: She looked at the setting and other signs, asked Tenzin how he felt, called the nurse and phoned his father.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's father see the phone call?
qa.a: He probably felt worried but grateful that the teacher noticed early and called him.

grounding: A child sweating on a cool day could be nervous or ill, and the teacher uses setting and other signs to decide.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
On Independence Day, my cousin Uday had to give a speech in front of the whole school in the Chennai heat. The sun was blazing, and everyone was sweating, even the principal.
But I noticed Uday more than the others. Sweat was running down his neck, and his hands were trembling around the paper. He kept looking at the crowd and then at his notes.
I couldn't tell if it was just the heat, or nerves, or both.
When he started speaking, his voice wobbled a bit. By the end, it was steady. Everyone clapped.
Afterwards he told me, "It was so hot, and I was so scared." Then he gulped a whole bottle of water.
- Aparna

qa.q: What were Uday's hands doing around the paper?
qa.a: They were trembling.

qa.q: What might Uday have been feeling while sweating and trembling?
qa.a: He was probably nervous about speaking to the whole school, though the heat also made everyone sweat, so Aparna couldn't be sure until he said so.

qa.q: What could Aparna look at to tell nerves from heat next time?
qa.a: Aparna could notice other signs like trembling hands, glancing between notes and crowd, and a wobbly voice, not just the sweat.

qa.q: How did the principal fit into the scene?
qa.a: The principal sweating too shows the heat affected everyone, so sweat alone couldn't show Uday's nerves.

grounding: An observer can't tell if a child's sweating is from heat or nerves until other signs and his own words make it clear.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
Saturday: Rekha came in from kho-kho with her fringe stuck to her forehead and sweat running down her neck. Her mother, Urmila, handed her water and laughed. "Who won?" "We did!"
Monday: Before the maths test, Rekha's palms were so damp that her pencil slipped. The fan was on and she hadn't run anywhere. She wiped her hands on her skirt and took a slow breath.
Thursday night: Rekha woke with her nightdress soaked, though the room was cool. She was shivering and her head ached. Urmila felt her forehead, sat with her, and in the morning took her to the doctor. On the way, Rekha said, "Three kinds of sweaty in one week." Urmila smiled. "And each one meant something different."

qa.q: What game had Rekha been playing on Saturday?
qa.a: Kho-kho.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling before the maths test when her palms were damp?
qa.a: She was nervous about the test; the fan was on and she hadn't been running, so the sweat most likely came from worry.

qa.q: What can help someone work out why a child is sweating?
qa.a: Looking at the setting and other signs, such as heat, a game, an upcoming test, or shivering and a headache, and getting a doctor's check when illness seems likely.

qa.q: How might Urmila have read Thursday night's sweat differently from Saturday's?
qa.a: On Saturday she saw a happy, hot child after a game; on Thursday the cool room, shivering and headache told her it was probably illness.

grounding: It shows the same sign, sweating, coming from exercise, test nerves and illness, with the setting and other signs telling them apart.
